title: Industrial Park Water Reset
note: МАКЕТ. Сценарий, тексты и веса — наши. Ни одного числа, имени и формулировки PrepMatter (Ф3). Развилки старого стиля: в ветку b ведут только слабые ходы, поэтому шесть экранов из шестнадцати видит лишь ошибающийся (Ф21). Не переписывается задним числом — свойство исчезает на библиотеке из шести сценариев.

intro.head: Welcome to the Sustainable Futures Lab
intro.body: You have joined a small team advising the operator of a large industrial park. You will make thirteen decisions. There is one clock for all of them, and you cannot go back.

intro.head: Background
intro.body: Riverside Industrial Park hosts eleven plants and draws all of its water from one river. The regional authority will cut the park's licensed withdrawal by 30% in eighteen months. Plant managers report their own water use monthly; the meters at the park boundary and the sum of plant reports have never matched. The park operator has asked your team to make the cut happen without stopping production.
intro.mission: Your mission: bring withdrawal down by 30% in eighteen months, keeping the plants running and the plant managers with you.

priorities.label: Form a working hypothesis about where the water actually goes
Get reliable measurement before anything else
Agree the target and the rules with the park operator
Talk to the plant managers who will have to change

steps.prompt: Put these four actions in the order you would take them, starting with the one you would do first.
steps.why: Гипотеза раньше замеров: без неё меряют всё подряд и тонут в данных. Согласование раньше разговора с цехами: без мандата обещания цехам ничем не обеспечены.

feedback.top: Your order puts a working hypothesis first. That is what keeps measurement finite: you look for the water you expect to find, and you notice fast when you are wrong.
feedback.mid: Your order is workable but spends early time on inputs before the team has a direction to test them against.
feedback.low: Your order gathers input and alignment before establishing an analytical direction. Without an initial hypothesis, measurement expands to fill the whole eighteen months.

steps.prompt: On day two, the park's environmental officer sends you a two-page note claiming that a single plant — the paper mill — accounts for most of the gap between the boundary meter and the plant reports. The note has no measurements attached.

options.text: You treat the note as one hypothesis among several and design your first week to test it against two other candidate explanations.
options.fb: You gave the note the weight it can carry — a lead, not a finding. Testing it beside two rivals is what makes the first week decisive rather than confirmatory.

options.text: You accept the note and focus the team's first week on the paper mill, taking the officer's read as the best local knowledge available on day two.
options.fb: A two-page note without measurements moved your whole week. If the officer is right you saved days; if wrong, you will find out only after the first week is gone.

options.text: You set the note aside and continue with the plan you had before it arrived.
options.fb: Ignoring a local expert's read costs you the cheapest lead you had. Steadiness is not the same as deafness.

options.text: You ask the officer for the underlying measurements before you decide anything, since a claim this specific is either well founded or quickly disproved.
options.fb: Asking for the data is right, but you stopped there: the week ran on while you waited for an answer that may not exist.

steps.prompt: The boundary meter reads 30% higher than the sum of the plant reports. Both numbers have been recorded the same way for four years. Two plants have no meter at all and estimate their use from production volume.

options.text: You take the boundary meter as the anchor and treat the plant reports as a decomposition to be corrected.
options.fb: One measured total and eleven self-reported parts: the total is the anchor, the parts are the estimate. That ordering resolves the conflict without new equipment.

options.text: You average the two figures to get a working number. The truth is unlikely to sit at either extreme and the board needs one line to plan against.
options.fb: Averaging a measurement with an estimate produces a number that describes neither. The gap was the finding; the average deletes it.

options.text: You commission new meters at all eleven plants before drawing any conclusion, on the view that a gap this large cannot be argued about until both sides of it are measured the same way.
options.fb: Correct eventually, but it buys certainty with months you do not have. The anchor was already on site.

options.text: You treat the two unmetered plants as the whole explanation of the gap: they are the only users nobody can put a figure on, and the gap has to sit somewhere.
options.fb: Two unmetered plants are the obvious suspect, and that is exactly why it deserves a check before it becomes the answer.

steps.prompt: Your first pass shows three candidate sources of the gap: cooling water at the two largest plants, an old distribution loop that leaks, and unmetered cleaning cycles across the park. You have four weeks before the operator's board meets.

options.text: You size all three roughly first, then go deep only on the largest.
options.fb: Rough sizing before depth is what makes four weeks enough. You bought the right to ignore two of the three.

options.text: You start with the leaking loop because it is the easiest to investigate.
options.fb: Ease of investigation is not size of prize. You may spend the four weeks on the smallest of the three.

options.text: You spend the four weeks agreeing an access and sampling protocol with the two plant operators before any measurement, and let the loop repair be scoped in the meantime.
options.fb: Access has to be agreed and it is not four weeks of work. A protocol is a permission to start, and you have spent the period that was for starting on obtaining it.

B1a.prompt: Sizing says cooling water at the two largest plants is roughly two thirds of the gap. Both plants run continuous processes; changing their cooling means a planned shutdown of several days each.

options.text: You fold the cooling change into each plant's already-scheduled maintenance window, since a shutdown nobody has to grant is a shutdown that happens, even though part of the saving lands four months later.
options.fb: Four months of delay bought you the shutdown you were never going to be granted separately. That is trading the right variable.

options.text: You propose a separate shutdown as soon as one can be arranged, so the saving lands in this financial year rather than the next, and the target stops depending on a schedule you do not control.
options.fb: The saving is real and the plan is clean, but you are spending the goodwill of the two plants you will need most for eighteen months.

options.text: You drop the cooling option as too disruptive and look for savings elsewhere, on the view that a measure the plants will fight is a measure that arrives two years late.
options.fb: You removed two thirds of the prize because the first version of the plan was uncomfortable.

B1b.prompt: Four weeks in, the two largest plants have still not been examined and the loop repair is the only thing scoped — worth about a tenth of the gap. The board meets next week.

options.text: You present the loop as a first step and state that the main driver has not yet been sized.
options.fb: Naming what you have not done is what keeps a partial answer usable. The board can now decide with the gap in view.

options.text: You present the loop repair as the recommendation and leave the sizing question for later.
options.fb: A tenth of the gap presented as the answer will be read as the answer. That is how a board approves a plan that cannot reach its target.

options.text: You ask to postpone the board meeting until the sizing is done.
options.fb: Honest, but it spends the operator's calendar to fix your sequencing.

steps.prompt: In a working session, the youngest engineer on the client team says quietly that the cleaning cycles were doubled two years ago after an audit, and no one changed the reporting template afterwards. The plant managers in the room do not react.

options.text: You ask her to walk the room through what changed, and check her point against the boundary meter that evening, since the room has just been told the number is wrong.
options.fb: You did two things at once: made the room hear the quietest useful voice, and tested what it said. Either alone would have been half the move.

options.text: You thank her and note the point for the technical session, so the meeting keeps its agenda and the operator does not watch your team argue about measurement in front of him.
options.fb: The agenda survived and the lead cooled. In a room that did not react, 'later' usually means never.

options.text: You ask the plant managers whether that is true, since they run the cycles daily and nobody has yet asked the people whose shifts the number comes from.
options.fb: You handed the question to the people with the least incentive to confirm it, in front of the person who raised it.

steps.prompt: The operator's finance director wants the 30% cut delivered mostly through a tariff that charges plants for water above a quota. The environmental officer warns that a tariff without technical help will push the two smallest plants below viability.

options.text: You propose the tariff with a quota set per unit of production and a technical support fund for plants below a size threshold.
options.fb: You kept the instrument the finance director needs and removed the failure mode the officer named. Both objections were about the same design, not about each other.

options.text: You back the tariff exactly as proposed, on the view that the smallest plants are not material to a 30% target and that carving out exceptions in the first month teaches everyone to ask for one.
options.fb: They are not material to the number and they are decisive to whether the park accepts it.

options.text: You drop the tariff and propose voluntary reduction targets instead.
options.fb: Voluntary targets against a licensed cut in eighteen months is not a trade-off, it is a postponement.

options.text: You ask the operator to decide between the two positions.
options.fb: Escalating a design question as a political one is how teams hand back the part of the work they were hired for.

steps.prompt: Eight weeks in, the river authority publishes a draft rule that could tighten the cut from 30% to 40%. It is a draft, open for consultation for three months.

options.text: You keep the 30% plan and add a check, which measures would still be worth starting now if the cut became 40%, because that list is the same under both numbers.
options.fb: You did not re-plan for a draft, and you did not ignore it. Testing the current plan against the harsher world costs a day and buys the decision either way.

options.text: You re-plan for 40% now, to be safe, on the view that a plan built to the harder number survives the licence being read strictly and the easier one does not.
options.fb: A draft moved your target by a third. If the consultation softens it, you will have spent the park's credibility on a number nobody asked for.

options.text: You continue with the 30% plan and revisit it when the rule is final, on the view that re-planning against a draft spends real weeks against a number that may never arrive.
options.fb: Reasonable, but three months of consultation is exactly the window in which cheap optionality is bought.

B2a.prompt: The paper mill's manager refuses the cooling change, saying the risk to his output is his alone to carry. He does not report to the park operator on technical matters.

options.text: You ask him what evidence would change his mind, and offer to run that test on his terms at your cost.
options.fb: You cannot instruct him, so you bought the only thing that moves someone you do not control: a test he chose the terms of.

options.text: You ask the park operator to require the change through the licence agreement. The mandate exists precisely so that one plant cannot hold the target hostage to its own reading of the data.
options.fb: You converted an engineering disagreement into a contractual one with the manager you need for eighteen months.

options.text: You re-plan the target without his plant.
options.fb: Removing the largest plant from the plan removes the plan.

B2b.prompt: The plants have heard that a 40% figure is circulating. Two managers ask whether the target is 30% or 40%, and say they will wait for a straight answer before committing capital.

options.text: You tell them that the licensed number is 30%, that a draft exists, and which measures are unaffected either way, since those are the ones they can start today.
options.fb: Uncertainty stated precisely is workable; uncertainty implied is paralysing. You gave them the part of the plan that does not depend on the answer.

options.text: You tell them to plan for 40% so that nobody is caught out later, and take the view that a team asked twice for the same plan will trust the second number less than the first.
options.fb: You asked for commitment to a number that does not exist yet, from people whose trust is the scarce resource here.

options.text: You tell them the target is 30% and say nothing about the draft, since a draft that may never be issued is not a number a delivery team can act on.
options.fb: They will read the draft next week. What you save today in simplicity you pay back in credibility.

steps.prompt: The cleaning-cycle data finally arrives: eleven spreadsheets in four formats, three of them monthly and the rest per shift, with two plants reporting in cubic metres and the rest in litres.

options.text: You convert everything to one unit and one period, then check the three largest plants by hand, because the file will be quoted at the board and nobody there will re-do the arithmetic.
options.fb: Normalise, then hand-check the part that carries the answer. The hand-check is what separates a clean file from a correct one.

options.text: You normalise everything to one unit and one period and use the result as it comes, since eleven files reconciled by hand is a fortnight you do not have and the errors should wash out across plants.
options.fb: Right shape, no verification. Unit conversion errors survive normalisation and look tidy afterwards.

options.text: You use only the three plants that report in a usable format. A comparison built on numbers you have had to reconstruct is one the operator can dismantle in a meeting.
options.fb: You selected the data by convenience of format, which has nothing to do with where the water is.

steps.prompt: Twelve weeks in, you can account for 24 of the 30 points of reduction with measures the plants accept. The remaining 6 points have no candidate yet, and the operator asks whether to start implementing.

options.text: You start the 24 points now and keep a named workstream on the remaining 6 with a date to review.
options.fb: Starting what is agreed while the gap stays visible and owned is the difference between a phased plan and an unfinished one.

options.text: You wait until the full 30 points are designed, so implementation starts once and the operator is not asked to approve the same programme twice.
options.fb: You are holding eighteen months of schedule hostage to the last fifth of the answer.

options.text: You start the 24 and present them as the plan, on the view that a plan with a hole named in it invites the authority to fill the hole for you.
options.fb: Six points quietly dropped is how a plan meets its milestones and misses its target.

options.text: You start the 24 points and ask the operator to negotiate the remaining 6 with the authority, on the view that a gap named in a licence is a legal question rather than an engineering one.
options.fb: Possible, but you handed away the part of the problem you were closest to solving.

steps.prompt: The board wants a decision paper in five days. You could spend those days tightening the numbers on the 24 agreed points, or on building the case for how the last 6 will be found.

options.text: You spend them on the last 6, because that is the part the board cannot check for itself.
options.fb: You spent the scarce days where the decision actually hangs. Agreed measures defend themselves; the gap does not.

options.text: You spend them on tightening the 24, because that is what the paper mostly contains.
options.fb: You improved the part that was already accepted, and left the contested part as it was.

B3a.prompt: Your case for the last 6 points rests on re-using treated water between two plants — technically sound, but it makes each plant dependent on the other's schedule.

options.text: You propose it with an explicit fallback each plant can trigger alone, and say what the fallback costs.
options.fb: You priced the dependency instead of hiding it. That is what lets two reluctant plants sign the same page.

options.text: You propose it on technical merit and let the plants work out the scheduling between them.
options.fb: The technical case was never the obstacle. You left the actual decision to the two parties least able to make it together.

options.text: You drop it and present the plan as 24 points with a gap.
options.fb: Honest, but you spent five days finding an option and then declined to put it on the table.

B3b.prompt: The paper is tight on the 24 points and thin on the remaining 6. In the meeting a board member asks directly how the park reaches 30%.

options.text: You answer that 24 points are designed and 6 are not, name the two candidates you would test first, and ask for four weeks, because a dated gap is a plan and an undated one is a hole.
options.fb: Asked directly, you answered directly and turned the gap into a request. That is recoverable; a hedge would not have been.

options.text: You say the remaining 6 points will come from measures still being finalised, since naming an unfinished list in a licence report is how a soft commitment becomes a hard one.
options.fb: A phrase in place of an answer, in the one meeting where the gap was visible anyway.

options.text: You say that 24 points are the realistic ceiling and that the target itself should be renegotiated. A plan presented as complete when it is not is the one that fails in public eighteen months from now.
options.fb: You proposed changing the target in the twelfth week, on the strength of not having looked at the last fifth.

title: District Heat Handover
note: МАКЕТ. Сценарий, тексты и веса — наши. Ни одного числа, имени и формулировки PrepMatter (Ф3). Второй сценарий строится с другим ключом ранжирования, чем первый (Ф15): иначе тренажёр учит порядку, а не суждению. Развилки старого стиля: в ветку b ведут только слабые ходы, поэтому шесть экранов из шестнадцати видит лишь ошибающийся (Ф21). Не переписывается задним числом — свойство исчезает на библиотеке из шести сценариев.

intro.head: Welcome to the Sustainable Futures Lab
intro.body: You have joined a small team advising a municipal heating utility. You will make thirteen decisions. There is one clock for all of them, and you cannot go back.

intro.head: Background
intro.body: Northgate District Energy heats forty-one thousand flats in a northern port city from a single coal-fired plant. The plant's operating permit ends in twenty-four months and will not be renewed. Replacing it means a different supply mix, a higher tariff, and a vote by the ninety housing associations that represent every connected building. The consultation leading to that vote takes eight months and the period is set in law. The utility holds twelve years of hourly metering for every substation. Nobody inside the utility can say who signs off the capital.
intro.mission: Your mission: keep forty-one thousand flats warm through the winter after the permit ends, with a tariff the housing associations will vote for.

priorities.label: Fix decision rights and the budget line with the city
Open the tariff consultation with the housing associations
Form a view on which supply mix can be built in twenty-four months
Work through the metering archive before committing to numbers

steps.prompt: Put these four actions in the order you would take them, starting with the one you would do first.
steps.why: Порядок здесь задаётся сроками и необратимостью, а не логикой анализа. Права решения не определены — это неделя работы, и она разблокирует всё остальное, поэтому идёт первой. Консультация по тарифу длится восемь месяцев и укоротить её нельзя, поэтому она запускается раньше, чем известен ответ, а не после. Гипотеза о составе источников успевает созреть внутри этих восьми месяцев. Архив замеров никуда не денется и читается под уже сформулированный вопрос — иначе двенадцать лет часовых данных съедят те же восемь месяцев. Обрати внимание: в предыдущем сценарии верным был обратный порядок, и это не ошибка — там связывающим ограничением была неизвестность, здесь календарь.

feedback.top: Your order starts the two clocks you do not control — the approval question and the eight-month consultation — before the work you can compress. That is sequencing by lead time rather than by logic.
feedback.mid: Your order is defensible but spends early weeks on work you could have done later, while the eight-month consultation period sits untouched.
feedback.low: Your order does the analysis first and the fixed-duration items last. The archive and the supply question will still be there in month six; the eight months will not.

steps.prompt: In your first week you find that three people each believe they approve the capital: the utility's managing director, the city's deputy mayor for infrastructure, and the chair of the municipal energy committee. None of them has said so in writing.

options.text: You put the three of them in one room and leave with a written note of who decides what, signed the same day.
options.fb: One room and one signed note cost you an afternoon and removed the failure mode that kills projects like this in month twenty. Decision rights are cheapest to fix while nothing is yet at stake.

options.text: You work with the managing director, since the utility owns the asset, and keep the other two informed.
options.fb: You picked the most convenient of three claimants. The other two will discover their authority at the moment you need the money, and they will be right.

options.text: You send all three a memo setting out your reading of who decides what and ask for objections.
options.fb: A memo puts the question on the table without forcing an answer. Silence from a claimant is not agreement, and you will be reading it as one for the next two years.

options.text: You proceed with the analysis and settle the approval question once the options are clear.
options.fb: Leaving decision rights until the options are ready means the first real decision of the project is also the first argument about who is entitled to make it.

steps.prompt: The metering archive is complete for twelve years, but three substations were renumbered after a reorganisation six years ago and the archive does not record when. On the face of it, district peak load has fallen nine per cent since then.

options.text: You reconcile the three renumbered substations against billing records before using any figure from before the reorganisation.
options.fb: Nine per cent is either a real efficiency gain or three substations counted twice, and the plant you size depends on which. Reconciling first makes the whole twelve-year series usable rather than merely available.

options.text: You use only the last six years, which are clean, and take the view that a series you can defend line by line is worth more than a longer one you would have to explain every time it is questioned.
options.fb: Six clean years beat twelve dirty ones. You have also thrown away the only period in the record containing a winter colder than anything in your remaining sample.

options.text: You read the nine per cent as evidence that demand is easing and size the new plant accordingly.
options.fb: You have sized a twenty-year asset on a number that a clerical renumbering would explain entirely. If it is an artefact, the flats are cold in February.

options.text: You ask the metering team to confirm the fall and carry on in parallel.
options.fb: Asking is right and carrying on is right, but you did not say what you would do if the answer came back bad — so it will arrive too late to change anything.

steps.prompt: The tariff consultation runs eight months by law and the period cannot be shortened. You are four weeks in, the supply mix is still open, and nothing you would say to the housing associations about price is settled.

options.text: You open the consultation now on the question of principle, that the tariff has to change, and bring the mix in as it firms up, since the eight months run whether you use them or not.
options.fb: You started the eight-month clock with the part that is already true. The mix can arrive during the consultation; the eight months cannot be bought back at any price.

options.text: You hold the consultation until the mix is decided, so the associations receive one clear proposal rather than a moving one they have to keep re-reading.
options.fb: One clear proposal is worth a great deal, and you have spent months you do not have to avoid a conversation you could have opened with what you already knew.

options.text: You ask the city to seek a legal shortening of the consultation period, on the view that eight months of process against a two-year build is the constraint worth attacking first.
options.fb: You spent political capital trying to move a fixed constraint instead of working inside it. The answer will arrive months from now and it will be no.

B1a.prompt: Three months into the consultation, a resident asks the direct question at a public meeting: how much will the standing charge rise? Your modelling gives anything from twelve to thirty per cent depending on which mix is chosen.

options.text: You give the range, name what would put the answer at each end, and say when you will narrow it, since a number invented tonight is the one the room will hold you to in a year.
options.fb: A named range with named drivers is an answer. Withholding it would have been heard as knowing the number and hiding it, which is the more expensive mistake here.

options.text: You give the lower end. The cheaper mix is still available and a number that frightens the room tonight is one you spend the next year walking back.
options.fb: Twelve per cent is now the number in the room. Every point above it will be read as a broken promise rather than as a modelling result.

options.text: You say you cannot give a number until the mix is chosen, on the view that a figure quoted at a public meeting becomes the promise everything afterwards is measured against.
options.fb: Technically correct and politically costly: you convened a public meeting and arrived at it with nothing you were willing to say.

B1b.prompt: The mix is settled, and you now enter a process needing eight months with seven left. Regulatory guidance says a compressed timetable can be challenged by any single association, of which there are ninety.

options.text: You go to the associations with the shortfall stated and ask them to agree the compressed timetable in writing.
options.fb: Asking them to own the compression is the only version of this that survives a challenge, because the people entitled to object have put their names to not objecting.

options.text: You run the full standard process and accept that the permit deadline is missed by a month.
options.fb: A month past the permit is not a schedule variance, it is a month with no lawful heat source. Someone else will discover that in November.

options.text: You start the compressed process and deal with a challenge if one comes.
options.fb: One association out of ninety can stop this, and you have handed each of them both a reason and a right to do it.

steps.prompt: Two mixes reach the target. A large heat pump array is far cheaper to run, but the network operator will only guarantee the grid connection in thirty months. A biomass boiler can be built in fifteen months and costs about forty per cent more to run over the next decade.

options.text: You take biomass for the first winters and design the site so the heat pump array can replace it later.
options.fb: The operating premium buys the one thing that cannot be bought later, which is heat in the first winter. Designing for the swap keeps the cheaper answer alive instead of trading it away.

options.text: You take the heat pump array and ask the network operator to accelerate the connection.
options.fb: Your plan now depends on another organisation beating its own guarantee, and their incentive to do that is nothing at all.

options.text: You take biomass and close the question, so that the whole organisation stops re-litigating the supply decision and starts on the twenty-four months of work that actually have to happen.
options.fb: The right first move, made irreversible for no reason. In ten years the operating premium is the largest single line in the budget and nobody can remember why.

options.text: You keep both options open until the network operator confirms.
options.fb: Optionality is worth paying for up to a point, and past that point it is a way of not deciding. With fifteen months of build ahead of you, you are past it.

steps.prompt: Eleven of the ninety associations hold a third of the flats between them and have voted as a block on every previous tariff question. Their chair tells you privately that they will support the change if the increase is phased over three years.

options.text: You test whether phasing works financially, and if it does, you arrange for it to arrive as their proposal rather than yours, because a concession they own is one they defend to the other seventy-nine.
options.fb: A concession that arrives as their idea survives being challenged in public. You also established it was affordable before you owed anybody anything.

options.text: You accept the phasing on the spot to lock in a third of the vote, on the view that a block which has voted together on every previous tariff question will not be won twice.
options.fb: You bought a third of the vote with a promise you have not costed, and the other two thirds have just learned what a private conversation with you is worth.

options.text: You decline, because a private arrangement with a block would look like one.
options.fb: Even-handedness is a real value, and you have spent your cheapest route to a majority buying it at full price.

steps.prompt: Fourteen months out, the parent company of your biomass fuel supplier enters administration. Your contract is with the subsidiary, which is still trading and still delivering on time.

options.text: You keep the contract running and spend two weeks securing a second supplier at a worse price, because the cost of the worse price is smaller than one cold week.
options.fb: You bought insurance while it was still cheap and without stopping anything that was working. The worse price is what certainty costs at the moment you still have a choice.

options.text: You terminate and re-tender the fuel contract immediately, on the view that a supplier who misses on the first winter will miss on the fifth.
options.fb: A parent in administration is a warning, not a default. You have paid for a re-tender and thrown away a supplier who is still delivering on time, on the strength of a headline.

options.text: You continue as planned and monitor the administration closely, since the subsidiary is trading, delivering on time, and holds the only contract priced inside your business case.
options.fb: Monitoring is not a plan. If the subsidiary is sold in month sixteen you will be tendering for fuel in the same quarter you are commissioning the boiler.

B2a.prompt: The second supplier quotes delivery reliability of ninety-nine point two per cent, measured across their entire book. Their contracts in this region are a tenth of that book and almost all of them are summer-weighted.

options.text: You ask for the regional winter subset before signing and treat the headline figure as unusable until you have it.
options.fb: A figure averaged over the wrong population is not a conservative estimate — it is a different question answered confidently. The subset you asked for is the only one your winters live in.

options.text: You accept the quoted figure and add a penalty clause for missed deliveries.
options.fb: A penalty converts a supply failure into money, and money does not heat a flat in January.

options.text: You accept the figure as it stands, since it has been audited.
options.fb: Audited means the arithmetic was checked, not that the population behind it resembles yours.

B2b.prompt: Commissioning tests return boiler efficiency two points under specification. The test week fell in an unseasonal warm spell and the unit spent most of it cycling on and off rather than running under steady load.

options.text: You re-test under load before accepting or rejecting the unit, since the test week that produced the number never put the unit under one.
options.fb: Cycling depresses measured efficiency, so the test answered a question you did not ask. One week of re-testing decides how a twenty-year asset is operated.

options.text: You accept the two-point shortfall and adjust the fuel budget. Two points is inside the noise of any single test week and the schedule has none to give.
options.fb: You have written a permanent line into the operating budget on the strength of a single unrepresentative week.

options.text: You reject the unit and invoke the performance guarantee now, on the view that a shortfall accepted at commissioning is a shortfall you own for the whole twenty-year life of the asset.
options.fb: Invoking a guarantee on a contested measurement starts a dispute you may well lose, in the one quarter you cannot afford to be in it.

steps.prompt: The city offers a grant covering a fifth of the capital cost. It carries one condition: the tariff must stay flat for the first two years after commissioning, which moves roughly the same amount onto years three to five.

options.text: You take the grant and put the deferred increase in front of the associations before the vote, not after it, because they will find it in year three either way.
options.fb: The money is worth having, and the deferral is only a trap if it arrives as a surprise. Showing it before the vote turns it into a choice they made rather than a bill they were sent.

options.text: You take the grant and present the flat first two years, since that is what the associations are being asked to vote on and the later path can be explained when it arrives.
options.fb: You have described the half of the condition that helps you. The other half arrives in year three with your signature on it and nobody else's.

options.text: You decline the grant to keep the tariff path simple, since a single increase the associations can understand is easier to vote for than a smaller one that grows again in year three.
options.fb: Simplicity is worth something, and here you have paid a fifth of the capital cost to buy it.

steps.prompt: Eight months out, four things are open — the fuel supply contract, the grid connection for the future heat pumps, a disputed easement across one site and the customer communications plan. Between them they need about fourteen weeks of your team and you have eight. Three of the four are dated by the commissioning day; the grid connection is dated by the network operator's quarterly connection window.

options.text: You book the window after next for the grid connection and put the freed weeks into the easement and the fuel contract.
options.fb: Three of these dates are yours and one belongs to somebody else's calendar — and the borrowed one is the only date that moves without moving commissioning. Choosing the later window is a decision with a date on it; the other three then fit in eight weeks.

options.text: You spend the eight weeks on the easement and on getting the grid connection application ready for the coming window, and leave the fuel contract and the communications plan to the final months.
options.fb: Both of those carry somebody else's clock and you have handled them properly. What you have pushed into the final months is the pair that decides commissioning and the vote: an unsigned supply contract stops the plant exactly as an unsettled easement does, and the associations meet the plan when there is no time left to change it.

options.text: You ask the city for two more people for the eight weeks and hold all four items on the dates they carry now.
options.fb: Two people found, cleared and briefed inside eight weeks are two people useful in the last three. Asking for capacity works when the ask comes before the crunch; this one arrives inside it, and the four dates do not move meanwhile.

options.text: You hand the easement to the city legal department and keep the other three in the team. The land question is theirs to begin with.
options.fb: It is their land question and it is your commissioning date. The city's lawyers work a queue with no commissioning date in it, and unlike the network operator they have no window you can book — you have put a blocker into a line with no number on it.

steps.prompt: Two months before the permit expires the boiler is three weeks behind. The coal plant could run four extra weeks under an emergency derogation the deputy mayor is willing to request, at the cost of the city's own emissions pledge for the year.

options.text: You ask for the derogation and publish the reason and the exact end date at the same time, since an exception with a date on it is the only kind a city can defend.
options.fb: The derogation was the only option that keeps the flats warm. Publishing the end date alongside it is what stops a four-week exception from quietly becoming a precedent.

options.text: You ask for the derogation and keep it quiet to avoid embarrassing the city, since the deputy mayor is spending his own credit to get it for you.
options.fb: A quiet exception is one leak away from being the story, and at that point it stops being a contingency and becomes a concealment.

options.text: You refuse the derogation and compress commissioning into the two months that remain, on the view that a city which breaks its own emissions pledge the first time it is inconvenient will not be believed the next time.
options.fb: You protected an annual pledge by putting an untested boiler into February with nothing behind it.

B3a.prompt: The derogation is granted and published. In the third of its four weeks commissioning is going well, and your team asks whether to hand over early or spend the remaining week on a full winter-load test.

options.text: You spend the week on the load test and hand over on the published date.
options.fb: That week was already paid for politically. Spending it on the test is the difference between a handover and a handover that holds in February.

options.text: You hand over early to show that the exception was shorter than the one you asked for, since the political credit from returning unused time is the thing that makes the next request possible.
options.fb: An early handover is a good headline and a poor engineering decision. You have given back the only slack anybody was ever going to grant you.

options.text: You spend the week on the test and ask for a further two weeks to be safe.
options.fb: Asking twice turns a bounded exception into an open-ended one, and the second request is the one that gets refused in public.

B3b.prompt: Handover happens with the unit two weeks proven rather than the six its specification assumes. The first hard cold snap is forecast for the month after.

options.text: You keep the commissioning team on site through the first cold snap and say publicly that you are doing so.
options.fb: Proving the unit in the weather it was bought for is the test you skipped, and doing it with the team on site converts an exposure into a plan people can see.

options.text: You release the commissioning team on schedule and rely on the maintenance contract.
options.fb: A maintenance contract promises a response within hours. Hours into a heat failure during a cold snap, this is already a public event.

options.text: You keep the team on site and say nothing, so as not to signal doubt.
options.fb: The precaution is right and the silence wastes it: nobody gives you credit for covering a risk they were never told about.

axis.none: замер круга 40: во всём видимом тексте нет ни одного числа с единицей — объявлять нечего. Это не освобождение: класс G краснеет, как только величина заведётся.

title: Harbour Silt Window
note: МАКЕТ. Сценарий, тексты и веса — наши. Ни одного числа, имени и формулировки PrepMatter (Ф3). Развилки ветвят по РОДУ хода, а не по его качеству (Ф21): в каждую ветку ведёт и сильный ход, и слабый, поэтому сильный кандидат тоже видит обе.

intro.head: Welcome to the Sustainable Futures Lab
intro.body: You have joined a small team advising a port authority. You will make thirteen decisions. There is one clock for all of them, and you cannot go back.

intro.head: Background
intro.body: The approach channel at Kelvinmouth has silted up. The draught limit now forces the two largest container lines to sail part-loaded, and one of them has told the port it will re-route within eighteen months. Dredging is permitted only inside a fourteen-week winter window set by the fisheries authority; miss it and the next one is a year away. Nobody knows what is in the sediment: the port's own survey is eleven years old and predates the closure of a chemical works upstream. Disposal of contaminated material costs about six times what clean material costs, and the laboratory analysis that settles the question takes eight weeks.
intro.mission: Your mission: get the channel dredged inside the winter window, without a disposal bill the port cannot carry and without losing the fishing co-op.

priorities.label: Survey what is actually in the sediment
Form a view on where the dredged material can go
Secure the dredging licence and the budget line from the port board
Sit down with the fishing co-op before anything is announced

steps.prompt: Put these four actions in the order you would take them, starting with the one you would do first.
steps.why: Здесь замеры идут первыми — и это не противоречит первому сценарию, а следует из другого ограничения. В «Industrial Park Water Reset» мерить можно было бесконечно, поэтому гипотеза задавала замерам границу. Здесь замер ровно один, он длится восемь недель и разводит стоимость вывоза в шесть раз. Пока проба не сдана, ни один следующий вопрос не имеет ответа: куда везти грунт — зависит от того, что в нём; сколько просить у совета — зависит от того же; что обещать рыбакам — тем более. Восемь недель лаборатории внутри четырнадцатинедельного окна — это и есть настоящий срок проекта, и он запускается в первый день или не запускается вовсе.

feedback.top: Your order starts the eight-week clock that every other answer waits on. Nothing downstream can be decided while the sediment is an open question, and the window will not move to accommodate the delay.
feedback.mid: Your order is workable, but it does useful work in a sequence where the laboratory result is still pending — and that result can invalidate it.
feedback.low: Your order leaves the survey until after the direction is set. If the sediment comes back contaminated, the plan you built in the meantime is the wrong plan and the window has moved closer.

steps.prompt: The chair of the fishing co-op hears about the project from a shipping newsletter rather than from the port, and says so publicly on day three.

options.text: You go to him the same week, say that he should have heard it from the port, and ask what he needs to see before anything is announced.
options.fb: Naming the failure yourself is what stops it becoming the story. You also converted an ambush into a standing channel, which is the only thing that will hold when the disposal figure arrives.

options.text: You issue a correction explaining that no decision has been taken, that consultation was always planned for a later stage, and that the newsletter drew conclusions the port had not reached.
options.fb: Everything in the statement is true and none of it answers his objection, which was about being told last rather than about the timetable.

options.text: You invite the co-op onto the project steering group so they see everything as it happens.
options.fb: Access is real and it is generous, and it also hands them a seat before you know what the sediment contains. You may be inviting them to watch you discover very bad news.

options.text: You let it pass and focus on the survey. The substance has not changed and the newsletter will be forgotten.
options.fb: The first thing the co-op learned about this project is that they learn about it from strangers, and nothing since has contradicted that.

steps.prompt: The eleven-year-old survey shows contamination well inside limits at every one of its nine sampling points. All nine sit in the outer channel; the inner basin, closest to the old chemical works, was never sampled.

options.text: You treat the old survey as evidence about the outer channel only, and design the new sampling around the basin it never covered.
options.fb: Nine clean readings are nine clean readings about the places they were taken. The value of the old survey is that it tells you where you do not need to look twice.

options.text: You treat the old survey as a reasonable baseline and sample lightly to confirm it, keeping the laboratory bill down.
options.fb: You are confirming a result in the one area where it was never in doubt, and skipping the area where the whole question lives.

options.text: You discard the eleven-year-old survey entirely as too old to carry any weight and sample the whole channel from scratch, on the view that a defensible plan cannot rest on readings taken before the works upstream closed.
options.fb: Defensible, and it spends laboratory weeks re-establishing something you already know. Age makes a survey less reliable; it does not make it worthless.

options.text: You ask the environmental regulator which sampling plan they would accept, and follow it.
options.fb: Their plan will certainly be accepted, which is worth a lot. It will also be built for their question rather than yours, and yours is where the six-fold cost sits.

steps.prompt: The laboratory will not report for eight weeks. Your team has that time and cannot spend it waiting. Two lines of work are open and you can staff one properly.

options.text: You spend the eight weeks designing the disposal route for the contaminated case, since that is the branch that can stop the project on cost.
options.fb: You prepared the expensive branch while it was still free to prepare. If the result comes back clean you have lost eight weeks of a plan you no longer need; if it comes back dirty you have the only eight weeks that existed.

options.text: You spend the eight weeks with the shipping lines, pinning down exactly what draught they need and by when, since the target itself is still an assumption.
options.fb: The whole project rests on a number nobody has verified, and you went and verified it. It is real work on the right question — it is simply not the question that can kill the budget.

options.text: You spend the eight weeks building the funding case for the dredging budget so the request is ready whichever way the laboratory reports, taking the draught target from what the shipping lines have already told the port.
options.fb: A funding case built before the disposal branch is priced leaves out the largest number in it, and the draught figure you borrowed is the one nobody has tested. Eight weeks produced a document that has to be rewritten twice.

B1a.prompt: Your disposal work finds only one licensed site within economic distance, and it has capacity for roughly half the volume. Its operator will hold that capacity for you, but only against a booking fee paid now — before the laboratory reports.

options.text: You pay the fee and book the capacity, and say at the board that it is insurance you may waste.
options.fb: The fee buys the only capacity that exists at a moment when it is still available. Calling it insurance rather than a plan is what keeps the board's trust when the result comes back clean and the money is gone.

options.text: You wait for the laboratory result before committing money to a problem that may not exist.
options.fb: Perfectly prudent, and the capacity is not reserved for your convenience. If the result is bad you will be looking for a site that has just been taken.

options.text: You ask the operator to hold it informally on the strength of the relationship.
options.fb: An informal hold is worth exactly what the next paying customer offers for it, and you will find that out on the worst possible day.

B1b.prompt: The eight weeks pass without the disposal route being worked, and the shipping lines produce an uncomfortable number of their own: the line threatening to leave needs a metre more draught than the dredging plan was scoped to deliver, and the second line needs half a metre less than assumed.

options.text: You re-scope around the deeper requirement and put the extra cost in front of the board with the re-routing risk beside it.
options.fb: The number that matters is the one that keeps the customer who is leaving. Putting the cost and the risk on the same page is what lets the board decide rather than react.

options.text: You keep the original scope, since it satisfies one line fully and the other nearly.
options.fb: The line it nearly satisfies is the line that has already said it will leave. A plan that misses its only binding customer has no purpose.

options.text: You ask the deeper line to confirm the requirement in writing before changing anything.
options.fb: Getting it in writing is right and it costs you two weeks of a fourteen-week window. Worth it once — not worth it for every number in the project.

steps.prompt: The board can fund either the full channel depth in one winter, or two thirds of it now with the remainder in the following window. The single-winter option needs a contingency line the finance director has never approved for a project of this size.

options.text: You put the single winter forward with the contingency named and a stated trigger for when it would be drawn.
options.fb: A contingency with a named trigger is a decision the board can take; a contingency without one is a blank cheque they will refuse. Same money, different question.

options.text: You propose the two-winter version, since it fits inside approvals the finance director already grants and gets a dredger into the water this year rather than into a board argument.
options.fb: It will be approved, and it also means the departing shipping line watches a second winter go by before the channel reaches the depth it asked for.

options.text: You propose the single winter and leave the contingency out of the paper to avoid a fight you might lose.
options.fb: The fight is not avoided, only postponed to the point where the money is needed and the board learns it was never asked for.

options.text: You ask the finance director privately what would have to be true for her to approve the contingency, and build the paper around her answer.
options.fb: The right conversation, and it makes the proposal hers as much as yours. It also risks producing a paper shaped to what she will approve rather than to what the channel needs.

steps.prompt: The fishing co-op's real objection turns out not to be the dredging itself but the plume: sixty boats fish the ground immediately outside the channel and expect it to be unfishable for a season.

options.text: You commission independent plume modelling with the co-op choosing one of the two modellers, and agree in advance what result would mean stopping.
options.fb: Letting them pick a modeller costs you nothing and buys the one thing you cannot buy later, which is that they believe the answer. Agreeing the stopping rule before the number arrives is what makes it a rule rather than an argument.

options.text: You offer compensation for the affected season, priced from their own landings records, so that the cost of the plume falls on the port rather than on sixty boats.
options.fb: Money for a lost season is fair and it settles the wrong dispute: they are telling you the ground may not come back, and you have answered as if it certainly will.

options.text: You point out that the modelling the regulator requires will settle the question anyway, and wait for it rather than running a second study the co-op did not ask for.
options.fb: The regulator's model will be technically sound and, to sixty skippers, it will be the port's model presented by the port's regulator.

steps.prompt: The laboratory reports. Contamination is above the disposal threshold in the inner basin and below it everywhere else — but the basin readings sit close enough to the line that a different laboratory could plausibly place them on the other side.

options.text: You plan for the contaminated case and commission a second laboratory, so the plan is not waiting on the appeal.
options.fb: You took the expensive reading seriously and tested it at the same time, which is the only version of this that costs weeks rather than a window.

options.text: You accept the result as given and re-plan the whole project around contaminated disposal, since an appeal can outlast the window.
options.fb: Decisive and defensible, and you have accepted a six-fold cost on a reading that sits close enough to the line to be worth one challenge.

options.text: You challenge the reading first and hold the plan until the second opinion arrives.
options.fb: The challenge is reasonable; stopping the plan for it is not. If the second laboratory agrees with the first, you have bought certainty with the weeks you needed to act on it.

B2a.prompt: A second laboratory returns readings below the threshold on the same basin material. The two laboratories used different extraction methods, and both are accredited for this work.

options.text: You put both results and both methods to the regulator and ask which method governs, rather than choosing the answer you prefer.
options.fb: Two accredited results disagreeing is a question about method, not about truth, and only the regulator can close it. Choosing for yourself would have made every later number arguable.

options.text: You use the lower result. It is the more recent of the two and equally accredited.
options.fb: Recency is not a tie-breaker between methods, and a disposal plan built on the cheaper of two contested readings will be challenged by the first person who wants it stopped.

options.text: You commission a third laboratory to break the tie.
options.fb: A third opinion produces a majority and not an answer: if it uses a third method you now have three results and the same open question, several weeks later.

B2b.prompt: Two days after you re-plan around contaminated disposal, the fisheries authority publishes next winter's window dates. It opens two weeks later than this year and closes on the same day — the working window has shrunk from fourteen weeks to twelve.

options.text: You re-plan for twelve weeks immediately and identify what comes out of scope, before a single contract is signed against the old dates.
options.fb: The window is the one input in this project that nobody negotiates. Re-planning against it while you still have a choice about what to drop is the difference between a decision and an announcement.

options.text: You ask the fisheries authority to reconsider the later opening, given the port's economic case.
options.fb: The dates are set by spawning, not by the port's calendar, and asking for an exception is how you spend the goodwill you will need for the plume conversation.

options.text: You hold the twelve-week problem until the disposal contract is signed, so that you re-plan once rather than twice.
options.fb: Sensible sequencing in a project that had time. Here you would be signing a contract priced against fourteen weeks of work you no longer have.

steps.prompt: The dredging contractor offers a rate roughly a fifth below the others. Their method moves more material per day and produces a heavier plume; the licence permits it, and the co-op has not been told the method is on the table.

options.text: You put the method to the co-op before you price it, and let their response decide whether it stays in the tender, since a saving they find out about afterwards costs more than it ever saved.
options.fb: The saving is real and it is not yours to bank quietly: the cost of the heavier plume lands on sixty boats. Asking first is also the only version where the saving survives being discovered.

options.text: You take the cheaper method: the licence permits it, the plume modelling will cover it, and a fifth off the dredging is real money back to the port.
options.fb: You have used the co-op's agreement to a process as agreement to an outcome they were never shown. The first skipper who reads the tender will say so publicly, and be right.

options.text: You reject the cheaper method outright to protect a relationship you have spent three months building, and take the higher price as the cost of not reopening the plume question.
options.fb: Protective and it spends a fifth of the dredging budget on a conversation you did not have. They might have accepted it for a share of the saving.

steps.prompt: Six weeks before the window opens, four things are unfinished: the disposal contract, the plume monitoring plan, the berth closure schedule with the terminal operator, and the public communications pack. Your team can finish two.

options.text: You finish the disposal contract and the berth schedule, and give the plume monitoring plan and the communications pack a working draft.
options.fb: You sorted by what physically stops the first day of dredging. Monitoring and communications can be improved during the window; a dredger with nowhere to put the spoil cannot.

options.text: You finish the plume monitoring plan and the communications pack, and give the disposal contract and the berth schedule a working draft.
options.fb: The political risk is real and it is not what stops the dredger. You are defending a position that can still be argued during the window, at the cost of two that cannot.

options.text: You finish the disposal contract and the communications pack, and leave the berth schedule to the terminal operator.
options.fb: A reasonable split, and the berth schedule is the one item where the other party has no reason to hurry: their berths are working today.

options.text: You spend the six weeks pressing the disposal operator for a better rate rather than signing at the one you have, and leave the other three at the working drafts you hold.
options.fb: A rate can be re-opened after the window; the window cannot be moved. Six weeks later there is a better number, no signature, and nobody has closed a berth for a dredger that cannot start without both.

steps.prompt: Three weeks into the window, the dredger hits an obstruction that was not on any chart and loses four working days. Two ways of buying the time back are open, and they are different in kind rather than in degree.

options.text: You buy the time from the schedule: a second shift, funded from the money the project already holds against exactly this.
options.fb: This is what the contingency was described for, and drawing it exactly as described is what makes the next one grantable. You bought time with money, which is the trade this project can afford.

options.text: You buy the time from the scope: drop the shallowest section, which serves the smaller of the two shipping lines, and finish the rest inside the window.
options.fb: A clean trade and a real loss. You protected the customer who was leaving by disappointing the one who was staying, and that is a choice the board should have made rather than heard about.

options.text: You absorb the four days and accept finishing four days into the closed window, on the view that nobody counts the last week.
options.fb: The window is set by spawning and enforced by the authority that also licenses your next one. Four quiet days is how a port loses the following winter.

B3a.prompt: The second shift works nights. On the third night the co-op reports that the plume is visible from shore under the working lights, well outside the modelled footprint. The monitoring buoys show nothing unusual.

options.text: You stop the night shift for one tide, go out with two skippers and the monitoring team, and look at it.
options.fb: One tide is a cheap price for the difference between a disputed instrument and a shared observation. Whatever the buoys say afterwards, they will now be saying it to people who were there.

options.text: You send them the buoy data, which is the agreed measure and shows nothing outside the envelope.
options.fb: The agreed measure is agreed until it contradicts what people can see with their own eyes at night, and then it is the port's instrument.

options.text: You continue and log the observation for the post-project review.
options.fb: A logged observation is a record that you were told and continued, which is exactly how it will be read at the licence hearing for the next window.

B3b.prompt: The channel does not reach full depth this winter, and the smaller of the two shipping lines works that out from the survey published at the end of the window. They ask the port directly whether the larger line was kept at their expense.

options.text: You answer that it was, explain the four lost days and the window, and put a dated commitment for their section in the next window on the table.
options.fb: They already know the answer; the only question is whether they hear it from you. A dated commitment turns a betrayal into a sequence, and a sequence can be lived with.

options.text: You answer that the scope was reduced for operational reasons inside the window and that no customer was prioritised.
options.fb: One customer was prioritised, the decision was correct, and this sentence turns a defensible choice into something that looks like a lie the moment anyone compares the charts.

options.text: You say the sequencing decision sits with the board and refer them to it.
options.fb: Technically accurate, and it tells a customer who asked you a direct question that you would rather not be the one answering it.
